questions.q: In a healthy 70-kg adult male, total body water accounts for approximately 60% of body weight (42 L), with two-thirds located in the intracellular fluid. Which cation is the principal osmotic determinant of intracellular fluid?
questions.explain: Potassium (K+, ~140-150 mEq/L) is the major intracellular cation maintained by Na+/K+-ATPase, whereas sodium (Na+, ~140 mEq/L) is the principal extracellular cation.

open.q: Name the predominant intracellular cation that determines intracellular fluid osmolality.

questions.q: Which protein accounts for nearly 80% of the colloid oncotic pressure of blood plasma, retaining fluid within the intravascular compartment?
questions.explain: Albumin is the most abundant plasma protein (~3.5-5.0 g/dL) and has a relatively low molecular weight (~66.5 kDa) with a high net negative charge, making it the primary contributor to plasma oncotic pressure.

open.q: Name the plasma protein responsible for generating approximately 80% of plasma colloid oncotic pressure.

questions.q: How does cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) composition normally differ from blood plasma?
options: CSF has much higher protein and glucose than plasma
CSF has lower chloride and magnesium than plasma
CSF has low protein, glucose below plasma, and relatively higher chloride and magnesium
CSF contains high concentrations of fibrinogen and bilirubin
questions.explain: The blood-CSF barrier restricts large plasma proteins (leaving CSF protein very low), and active choroid plexus transport maintains higher Cl- and Mg2+ in CSF, while glucose is roughly two-thirds of simultaneous blood glucose.

open.q: What is the normal approximate ratio of cerebrospinal fluid glucose to simultaneous blood glucose?

questions.q: Which buffer system is the most important extracellular chemical buffer in blood plasma, largely because its components can be independently regulated by the lungs and kidneys?
questions.explain: Although its pKa (6.1) is slightly below blood pH (7.4), the HCO3-/H2CO3 system is the primary physiological extracellular buffer because PaCO2 is rapidly adjusted by alveolar ventilation and HCO3- by renal tubules.

open.q: Name the primary physiological extracellular buffer system of blood plasma regulated by the lungs and kidneys.

questions.q: According to the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation for the bicarbonate buffer system (pH = 6.1 + log([HCO3-] / 0.03 x PaCO2)), what molar ratio of bicarbonate to dissolved carbon dioxide maintains a normal arterial blood pH of 7.40?
questions.explain: At normal values ([HCO3-] = 24 mEq/L and 0.03 x 40 mmHg = 1.2 mmol/L), the ratio is 24 / 1.2 = 20:1, and 6.1 + log10(20) = 6.1 + 1.3 = 7.40.

open.q: What ratio of plasma bicarbonate concentration to dissolved carbon dioxide maintains a normal blood pH of 7.40?

questions.q: Which amino acid side chain on hemoglobin provides the majority of its physiological intracellular buffering capacity in red blood cells?
questions.explain: The imidazole side chain of histidine has a pKa near physiological pH (~6.8), allowing hemoglobin's numerous histidine residues to buffer H+ ions generated from tissue CO2 hydration (Haldane effect).

open.q: Name the amino acid residue whose imidazole side chain accounts for hemoglobin's strong intracellular buffering capacity.

questions.q: Which multimeric glycoprotein synthesized by endothelial cells and megakaryocytes bridges subendothelial collagen to platelet glycoprotein Ib (GpIb) receptors during primary hemostasis?
questions.explain: von Willebrand factor (vWF) binds exposed subendothelial collagen and platelet GpIb-IX-V receptors under high shear stress, while also stabilizing Factor VIII in plasma.

open.q: Name the multimeric adhesive glycoprotein that links subendothelial collagen to platelet GpIb receptors and stabilizes Factor VIII.

questions.q: Which platelet surface integrin receptor binds fibrinogen to crosslink adjacent platelets during platelet aggregation, and is deficient in Glanzmann thrombasthenia?
questions.explain: Activation of platelets induces a conformational change in GpIIb/IIIa, allowing bivalent fibrinogen molecules to bridge adjacent platelets; its deficiency causes Glanzmann thrombasthenia.

open.q: Name the platelet fibrinogen receptor required for platelet aggregation that is defective in Glanzmann thrombasthenia.

questions.q: How do endothelial prostacyclin (PGI2) and platelet thromboxane A2 (TXA2) exert opposing biochemical effects on platelet aggregation?
options: TXA2 promotes platelet aggregation; PGI2 raises platelet cAMP and inhibits aggregation
TXA2 raises platelet cGMP, whereas PGI2 lowers platelet cGMP
Both act through nuclear receptors to alter gene transcription
TXA2 cleaves fibrinogen, whereas PGI2 polymerises fibrin
questions.explain: Platelet COX-1 generates TXA2 (vasoconstrictor and platelet aggregator via Gq/Gi), whereas endothelial COX-2/prostacyclin synthase generates PGI2 (vasodilator and platelet inhibitor via Gs-mediated cAMP elevation).

open.q: Name the prothrombotic eicosanoid synthesized by platelets via COX-1 that promotes vasoconstriction and platelet aggregation.

questions.sub: Coagulation Cascade and Vitamin K-Dependent Factors
questions.q: Which four procoagulant clotting factors require vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation of N-terminal glutamate residues?
options: Factors I, V, VIII, and XIII
Factors II, VII, IX, and X
Factors XI, XII, prekallikrein, and HMWK
Factors III, IV, VIII, and vWF
questions.explain: Factors II (prothrombin), VII, IX, and X (plus anticoagulant proteins C and S) undergo gamma-glutamyl carboxylation so they can chelate Ca2+ and bind negatively charged platelet phospholipids.

open.q: List the four procoagulant clotting factors that depend on vitamin K for gamma-carboxylation.
accept: Factors II, VII, IX, and X

questions.sub: Coagulation Cascade and Vitamin K-Dependent Factors
questions.q: How does warfarin exert its anticoagulant effect at the enzymatic level?
options: Directly inhibits thrombin and factor Xa active sites
Inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, reducing active vitamin K regeneration
questions.explain: Warfarin blocks vitamin K epoxide reductase, halting the recycling of oxidized vitamin K epoxide back to the active reduced hydroquinone cofactor needed by gamma-glutamyl carboxylase.

open.q: Name the enzyme inhibited by warfarin to block recycling of vitamin K.

questions.sub: Coagulation Cascade and Vitamin K-Dependent Factors
questions.q: Which divalent cation (historically designated Factor IV) is essential for bridging gamma-carboxyglutamate (Gla) domains of clotting factors to negatively charged phosphatidylserine on activated platelets?
questions.explain: Calcium ions (Ca2+) form coordination bridges between negatively charged gamma-carboxyglutamate residues on Factors II, VII, IX, and X and exposed phosphatidylserine on activated platelet membranes.

open.q: Name the divalent cation essential as a cofactor in multiple steps of the coagulation cascade.

questions.sub: Coagulation Cascade and Vitamin K-Dependent Factors
questions.q: A 6-year-old boy presents with recurrent hemarthroses and prolonged bleeding after dental extraction. Laboratory tests show a normal PT, normal bleeding time, and markedly prolonged aPTT that corrects on a 1:1 mixing study. Deficiency of which factor is most common in this X-linked disorder?
questions.explain: Hemophilia A is an X-linked recessive deficiency of Factor VIII (intrinsic pathway cofactor for Factor IXa), causing deep tissue/joint bleeding and an isolated prolonged aPTT.

open.q: Deficiency of which coagulation factor causes X-linked hemophilia A?

questions.sub: Coagulation Cascade and Vitamin K-Dependent Factors
questions.q: Which coagulation factor is a transglutaminase activated by thrombin that crosslinks adjacent fibrin strands via covalent epsilon-(gamma-glutamyl)lysine isopeptide bonds to stabilize the fibrin clot?
questions.explain: Factor XIIIa (fibrin-stabilizing factor) forms covalent amide crosslinks between glutamine and lysine side chains of fibrin polymers, making the clot mechanically stable and resistant to plasmin.

open.q: Name the transglutaminase clotting factor that covalently crosslinks fibrin polymers to stabilize the blood clot.

questions.sub: Coagulation Cascade and Vitamin K-Dependent Factors
questions.q: Which coagulation complex initiates the extrinsic pathway in vivo upon vascular injury, and which laboratory test evaluates this pathway?
options: Factor XIIa-HMWK complex; activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT)
Tissue factor (Factor III)-Factor VIIa complex; prothrombin time (PT/INR)
questions.explain: Subendothelial tissue factor (Factor III) binds and activates Factor VII to Factor VIIa, activating Factor X and Factor IX; the extrinsic and common pathways are assessed clinically by the prothrombin time (PT/INR).

open.q: Name the coagulation test used clinically to monitor warfarin therapy and assess the extrinsic and common coagulation pathways.

questions.q: How does unfractionated heparin produce rapid anticoagulation in vivo?
options: Inhibits hepatic synthesis of vitamin K-dependent factors
Enhances antithrombin activity against thrombin and factor Xa
questions.explain: Heparin binds to a lysine-rich site on antithrombin III (ATIII), dramatically enhancing ATIII's ability to neutralize serine proteases, especially thrombin and Factor Xa.

open.q: Name the endogenous plasma serine protease inhibitor whose activity is accelerated 1,000-fold by heparin.

questions.q: How does the endothelial protein C pathway limit thrombus extension on intact vascular endothelium?
options: Thrombin-thrombomodulin activates protein C; activated protein C with protein S inactivates Va and VIIIa
Protein C activates Factors V and VIII to strengthen clots
Thrombomodulin converts plasminogen directly into fibrin
questions.explain: Intact endothelial cells express thrombomodulin, which switches thrombin's substrate specificity from fibrinogen to protein C; activated protein C (APC) with cofactor protein S cleaves and inactivates Factors Va and VIIIa.

open.q: Which two activated coagulation cofactors are proteolytically inactivated by activated protein C and protein S?

questions.q: A 29-year-old woman develops a deep vein thrombosis after starting oral contraceptives. Genetic testing reveals Factor V Leiden. What is the specific molecular abnormality in Factor V Leiden?
options: Complete absence of Factor V synthesis
Factor V Leiden resists inactivation by activated protein C because of an Arg506Gln substitution
questions.explain: Factor V Leiden replaces arginine with glutamine at position 506, eliminating the primary cleavage site for activated protein C (APC resistance) and causing inherited thrombophilia.

open.q: Name the inherited thrombophilia caused by a mutation in Factor V that confers resistance to inactivation by activated protein C.

questions.q: Which serine protease dissolves blood clots by cleaving crosslinked fibrin polymers into fibrin degradation products including D-dimers?
questions.explain: Tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) converts inactive zymogen plasminogen into active plasmin, which digests fibrin meshes and releases D-dimers from Factor XIIIa-crosslinked fibrin.

open.q: Name the active fibrinolytic enzyme derived from plasminogen that degrades fibrin clots.

questions.q: Why does an elevated plasma D-dimer level specifically indicate degradation of a stabilized fibrin clot rather than simple fibrinogenolysis?
options: D-dimer is synthesised directly by hepatocytes during inflammation
Unpolymerised fibrinogen contains preformed D-dimer epitopes
Plasmin generates D-dimer only from uncrosslinked fibrin monomers
D-dimer is released when plasmin degrades factor XIIIa-crosslinked fibrin
questions.explain: Free fibrinogen and uncrosslinked fibrin lack covalent bonds between adjacent D domains; D-dimer appears only when a thrombus has been crosslinked by Factor XIIIa and then degraded by plasmin.

open.q: Which fibrin degradation product specifically reflects plasmin cleavage of Factor XIIIa-crosslinked fibrin?
